questions.title: Room Tile Calculation
questions.objective: Return integer tile count given room dimension and optional tile size.
questions.problem_statement:
Task: Write a function tiles_needed(l, w, s=1) that tells how many square tiles are needed to cover a rectangular room.
• l and w are the length and width of the room
• s is the side length of one square tile (default value is 1)
• If a room side is not an exact multiple of the tile side, the last row or column still needs a whole tile, so round up in each direction
• Return the tile count as an integer

Example: tiles_needed(10, 10, 3) → 16, because 10 / 3 rounds up to 4 tiles in each direction (4 × 4 = 16).
questions.input_format:
Function signature: tiles_needed(l, w, s=1) -> int
Parameters:
• l: room length (positive integer)
• w: room width (positive integer)
• s: tile side length (positive integer, default 1)
Test format: each line of a test input is the argument list of one call (for example, 5, 4 means tiles_needed(5, 4)). The expected output is the repr of the returned value, one line per call.
questions.output_format: Return an int: the total number of tiles needed.
hints: Tiles needed along the length = ceil(l / s), and along the width = ceil(w / s).
Round up with integer maths: -(-l // s) or (l + s - 1) // s.
Multiply the two counts to get the answer.
questions.reference_solution:
def tiles_needed(l, w, s=1):
    rows = (l + s - 1) // s
    cols = (w + s - 1) // s
    return rows * cols

extra_fields.input_format:
Function signature: tiles_needed(l, w, s=1) -> int
Parameters:
• l: room length (positive integer)
• w: room width (positive integer)
• s: tile side length (positive integer, default 1)
Test format: each line of a test input is the argument list of one call (for example, 5, 4 means tiles_needed(5, 4)). The expected output is the repr of the returned value, one line per call.
extra_fields.output_format: Return an int: the total number of tiles needed.

questions.title: Better Deal Selector
questions.objective: Compare two discounted offerings and return 1 or 2 identifying the cheaper option.
questions.problem_statement:
Task: Write a function better_deal(p1, d1, p2, d2) that compares two offers. Offer 1 has price p1 with a discount of d1 percent. Offer 2 has price p2 with a discount of d2 percent.
• Final price = price x (100 - discount) / 100
• Return 1 if offer 1 has the lower final price
• Return 2 if offer 2 has the lower final price
• If both final prices are equal, return 1

Example: better_deal(1000, 20, 900, 5) → 1, because the final prices are 800 and 855.
questions.input_format:
Function signature: better_deal(p1, d1, p2, d2) -> int
Parameters:
• p1: price of offer 1 (positive integer)
• d1: discount of offer 1 in percent (integer, 0 to 100)
• p2: price of offer 2 (positive integer)
• d2: discount of offer 2 in percent (integer, 0 to 100)
Test format: each line of a test input is the argument list of one call (for example, 1000, 20, 900, 5 means better_deal(1000, 20, 900, 5)). The expected output is the repr of the returned value, one line per call.
hints: You can compare p1 * (100 - d1) with p2 * (100 - d2) and skip the division by 100.
Using integers only avoids rounding errors.
Use <= so that an equal price returns 1.

extra_fields.input_format:
Function signature: better_deal(p1, d1, p2, d2) -> int
Parameters:
• p1: price of offer 1 (positive integer)
• d1: discount of offer 1 in percent (integer, 0 to 100)
• p2: price of offer 2 (positive integer)
• d2: discount of offer 2 in percent (integer, 0 to 100)
Test format: each line of a test input is the argument list of one call (for example, 1000, 20, 900, 5 means better_deal(1000, 20, 900, 5)). The expected output is the repr of the returned value, one line per call.

questions.title: Seconds to Duration String
questions.objective: Return formatted duration string "Xh Ym Zs" from integer seconds.
questions.problem_statement:
Task: Write a function format_duration(sec) that converts a number of seconds into hours, minutes and seconds.
• 1 hour = 3600 seconds and 1 minute = 60 seconds
• Return a string in this exact format: "Xh Ym Zs" (for example "1h 1m 1s")
• Always show all three parts, even when a part is 0
• Hours are not limited to 24

Example: format_duration(3661) → "1h 1m 1s". Example: format_duration(100000) → "27h 46m 40s".
questions.input_format:
Function signature: format_duration(sec) -> str
Parameters:
• sec: number of seconds (non-negative integer)
Test format: each line of a test input is the argument list of one call (for example, 3661 means format_duration(3661)). The expected output is the repr of the returned value, one line per call.
hints: divmod(sec, 3600) gives the hours and the remaining seconds.
Use divmod again on the remaining seconds with 60 to get minutes and seconds.
Build the string with an f-string: f"{h}h {m}m {s}s".
questions.reference_solution:
def format_duration(sec):
    h, rest = divmod(sec, 3600)
    m, s = divmod(rest, 60)
    return f"{h}h {m}m {s}s"

extra_fields.input_format:
Function signature: format_duration(sec) -> str
Parameters:
• sec: number of seconds (non-negative integer)
Test format: each line of a test input is the argument list of one call (for example, 3661 means format_duration(3661)). The expected output is the repr of the returned value, one line per call.

questions.title: Numeric Palindrome Predicate
questions.objective: Return Boolean indicating whether an integer reads the same forwards and backwards.
questions.problem_statement:
Task: Write a function is_num_pal(n) that returns True if an integer reads the same forwards and backwards, and False otherwise.
• Use maths only (// and %). Do not convert the number to a string
• Negative numbers are never palindromes
• 0 is a palindrome

Examples: is_num_pal(121) → True, is_num_pal(10) → False, is_num_pal(-121) → False.
questions.input_format:
Function signature: is_num_pal(n) -> bool
Parameters:

Test format: each line of a test input is the argument list of one call (for example, 121 means is_num_pal(121)). The expected output is the repr of the returned value, one line per call.
questions.output_format: Return a bool: True or False.
hints: Return False at once if n is negative.
Reverse a copy of n with a loop: rev = rev * 10 + n % 10, then n //= 10.
Compare the reversed number with the original number.

extra_fields.input_format:
Function signature: is_num_pal(n) -> bool
Parameters:
• n: an integer
Test format: each line of a test input is the argument list of one call (for example, 121 means is_num_pal(121)). The expected output is the repr of the returned value, one line per call.
extra_fields.output_format: Return a bool: True or False.

questions.title: Compound Interest Return
questions.objective: Compute compound return given principal, annual rate, and years.
questions.problem_statement:
Task: Write a function compound_int(p, r, t, n=1) that returns the final amount after compound interest.
• Formula: A = p x (1 + r / (100 x n)) ^ (n x t)
• p is the principal (starting money), r is the annual rate in percent (5 means 5%), t is the number of years
• n is how many times interest is added per year (default 1)
• Return A rounded to 2 decimal places

Example: compound_int(1000, 5, 2) → 1102.5, because 1000 × 1.05 ^ 2 = 1102.5.
questions.input_format:
Function signature: compound_int(p, r, t, n=1) -> float
Parameters:
• p: principal amount (positive number)
• r: annual interest rate in percent (non-negative number)
• t: number of years (non-negative integer)
• n: compounding periods per year (positive integer, default 1)
Test format: each line of a test input is the argument list of one call (for example, 1000, 5, 2 means compound_int(1000, 5, 2)). The expected output is the repr of the returned value, one line per call.
questions.output_format: Return a float: the final amount rounded to 2 decimal places.
hints: The rate per period is r / (100 * n), and the number of periods is n * t.
In Python the power operator is **.
Finish with round(result, 2).

extra_fields.input_format:
Function signature: compound_int(p, r, t, n=1) -> float
Parameters:
• p: principal amount (positive number)
• r: annual interest rate in percent (non-negative number)
• t: number of years (non-negative integer)
• n: compounding periods per year (positive integer, default 1)
Test format: each line of a test input is the argument list of one call (for example, 1000, 5, 2 means compound_int(1000, 5, 2)). The expected output is the repr of the returned value, one line per call.
extra_fields.output_format: Return a float: the final amount rounded to 2 decimal places.

questions.title: Scope Shadowing Trace
questions.objective: Predict return value when a local function variable shadows a global variable.
questions.problem_statement:
Task: A variable created inside a function is local. If it has the same name as a global variable, it shadows (hides) the global one inside the function, and the global value is not changed.

Assume your file starts with these two global variables:
level = 10
bonus = 5

Write a function compute_shadow(x) that follows these rules:
• Create a local variable named level inside the function and set it to x * 2 (this shadows the global level)
• Read the global variable bonus (do not create a local bonus)
• Return the local level plus bonus
• Do not use the global keyword. The global level must stay 10

Example: compute_shadow(4) → 13, because the local level is 8 and bonus is 5.
questions.input_format:
Function signature: compute_shadow(x) -> int
Parameters:
• x: an integer
The module already contains the globals level = 10 and bonus = 5.
Test format: each line of a test input is the argument list of one call (for example, 4 means compute_shadow(4)). The expected output is the repr of the returned value, one line per call.
hints: Assigning to a name inside a function makes that name local to the function.
Reading a name that is not assigned inside the function uses the global one.
So level = x * 2 is local, while bonus is read from the global scope.
questions.reference_solution:
level = 10
bonus = 5

def compute_shadow(x):
    level = x * 2
    return level + bonus

extra_fields.input_format:
Function signature: compute_shadow(x) -> int
Parameters:
• x: an integer
The module already contains the globals level = 10 and bonus = 5.
Test format: each line of a test input is the argument list of one call (for example, 4 means compute_shadow(4)). The expected output is the repr of the returned value, one line per call.

questions.title: Keyword-Only Invoicing
questions.objective: Enforce keyword-only parameters using * syntax to format user billing strings.
questions.problem_statement:
Task: In Python, every parameter written after a bare * in the parameter list is keyword-only: the caller must pass it by name.

Write a function format_inv(c, *, amt, rate=0.18) that builds a billing line.
• c is the customer name (a normal parameter)
• amt is the bill amount and must be passed by keyword, for example amt=1000
• rate is the tax rate (default 0.18) and must also be passed by keyword
• tax = amt x rate, and total = amt + tax
• Return exactly: Invoice for <c>: amount=<amt>, tax=<tax>, total=<total>, with each of the three numbers written with 2 decimal places
• If the caller passes amt without its keyword, as in format_inv('Asha', 1000), Python raises TypeError by itself. This is the expected behaviour

Example: format_inv('Asha', amt=1000) → "Invoice for Asha: amount=1000.00, tax=180.00, total=1180.00".
questions.input_format:
Function signature: format_inv(c, *, amt, rate=0.18) -> str
Parameters:
• c: customer name (string)
• amt: bill amount, keyword-only (non-negative number)
• rate: tax rate, keyword-only (default 0.18)
Test format: each line of a test input is the argument list of one call (for example, 'Asha', amt=1000 means format_inv('Asha', amt=1000)). The expected output is the repr of the returned value, one line per call.
questions.output_format: Return a str in the format: Invoice for <c>: amount=<amt>, tax=<tax>, total=<total>. If a call breaks the keyword-only rule, it raises TypeError (the expected output line is TypeError).
hints: A bare * in the parameter list makes every parameter after it keyword-only.
Format each number with f"{value:.2f}".
You do not need to write any code to raise the TypeError. Python does it for you.
questions.reference_solution:
def format_inv(c, *, amt, rate=0.18):
    tax = amt * rate
    total = amt + tax
    return f"Invoice for {c}: amount={amt:.2f}, tax={tax:.2f}, total={total:.2f}"

extra_fields.input_format:
Function signature: format_inv(c, *, amt, rate=0.18) -> str
Parameters:
• c: customer name (string)
• amt: bill amount, keyword-only (non-negative number)
• rate: tax rate, keyword-only (default 0.18)
Test format: each line of a test input is the argument list of one call (for example, 'Asha', amt=1000 means format_inv('Asha', amt=1000)). The expected output is the repr of the returned value, one line per call.
extra_fields.output_format: Return a str in the format: Invoice for <c>: amount=<amt>, tax=<tax>, total=<total>. If a call breaks the keyword-only rule, it raises TypeError (the expected output line is TypeError).

questions.title: Mutable Default Trap Demo
questions.objective: Demonstrate default argument trap contrasting None sentinel vs mutable list.
questions.problem_statement:
Task: A default argument value is created only once, when the function is defined. If the default is a mutable list ([]), the same list is shared by every call, so entries from earlier calls pile up. This is a common trap. The safe way is to use None as the default value and create a new list inside the function.

Write a function append_entry(e, led=None) that follows these rules:
• If led is None, start a new empty list for this call
• Append e to the list and return that list
• If a list is given in led, append e to that same list and return it
• Calls without led must never share data: append_entry(1) followed by append_entry(2) must return [1] and then [2]

Example: append_entry(5, [1, 2]) → [1, 2, 5].
questions.input_format:
Function signature: append_entry(e, led=None) -> list
Parameters:
• e: the entry to add (any value)
• led: the ledger, a list (default None)
Test format: each line of a test input is the argument list of one call (for example, 1
2
3 means append_entry(1), then append_entry(2), then append_entry(3)). The expected output is the repr of the returned value, one line per call.
questions.output_format: Return the list that contains the new entry as its last item.
questions.constraints: The list led, when given, holds at most 1000 items.
hints: Never write led=[] in the parameter list.
Use led=None, then check: if led is None: led = [].
Append e with led.append(e) and return led.

extra_fields.input_format:
Function signature: append_entry(e, led=None) -> list
Parameters:
• e: the entry to add (any value)
• led: the ledger, a list (default None)
Test format: each line of a test input is the argument list of one call (for example, 1
2
3 means append_entry(1), then append_entry(2), then append_entry(3)). The expected output is the repr of the returned value, one line per call.
extra_fields.output_format: Return the list that contains the new entry as its last item.

questions.title: Tax Slab Function
questions.objective: Calculate progressive income tax across 3 fictional brackets.
questions.problem_statement:
Task: Write a function calc_tax(income) that returns the income tax using progressive brackets. Each rate applies only to the part of the income that falls inside that bracket:
• First 250000: 0% tax
• From 250001 to 500000: 10% tax
• Above 500000: 20% tax
Return the total tax rounded to 2 decimal places.

Example: calc_tax(750000) → 75000.0. The tax is 0 on the first 250000, plus 10% of the next 250000 (= 25000), plus 20% of the last 250000 (= 50000).
questions.input_format:
Function signature: calc_tax(income: float) -> float
Parameters:
• income: annual income (non-negative number)
Test format: each line of a test input is the argument list of one call (for example, 750000 means calc_tax(750000)). The expected output is the repr of the returned value, one line per call.
questions.output_format: Return a float: the total tax rounded to 2 decimal places.
hints: Tax is marginal: only the slice of income inside a bracket uses that bracket's rate.
Work from the top bracket down: tax the part above 500000, then cut the income to 500000 and continue.
Return round(tax, 2). Start with tax = 0.0 so the result is always a float.

questions.title: Loan EMI Computation
questions.objective: Compute monthly loan repayment using standard EMI formula.
questions.problem_statement:
Task: EMI (equated monthly instalment) is the fixed amount you pay every month to repay a loan. Write a function calc_emi(p, r, n) that returns the EMI.
• p is the loan amount, r is the annual interest rate in percent, n is the number of months
• Monthly rate: R = r / 12 / 100
• Formula: EMI = p x R x (1 + R)^n / ((1 + R)^n - 1)
• Special case: if r is 0 there is no interest, so EMI = p / n
• Return the EMI rounded to 2 decimal places

Example: calc_emi(100000, 10, 12) → 8791.59.
questions.input_format:
Function signature: calc_emi(p, r, n) -> float
Parameters:
• p: loan amount (positive number)
• r: annual interest rate in percent (non-negative number)
• n: number of months (positive integer)
Test format: each line of a test input is the argument list of one call (for example, 100000, 10, 12 means calc_emi(100000, 10, 12)). The expected output is the repr of the returned value, one line per call.
questions.output_format: Return a float: the monthly EMI rounded to 2 decimal places.
hints: Compute the monthly rate once: R = r / 12 / 100.
Store (1 + R) ** n in a variable because it is used twice in the formula.
Handle r == 0 first so you never divide by zero.

extra_fields.input_format:
Function signature: calc_emi(p, r, n) -> float
Parameters:
• p: loan amount (positive number)
• r: annual interest rate in percent (non-negative number)
• n: number of months (positive integer)
Test format: each line of a test input is the argument list of one call (for example, 100000, 10, 12 means calc_emi(100000, 10, 12)). The expected output is the repr of the returned value, one line per call.
extra_fields.output_format: Return a float: the monthly EMI rounded to 2 decimal places.

questions.title: Leap Year Predicate
questions.objective: Return True if year is a Gregorian leap year, False otherwise.
questions.problem_statement:
Task: Write a function is_leap(year) that returns True if the year is a leap year in the Gregorian calendar, and False otherwise.
• A year divisible by 4 is a leap year
• Exception: a year divisible by 100 is NOT a leap year
• Exception to the exception: a year divisible by 400 IS a leap year

Examples: 2024 → True, 2023 → False, 1900 → False (divisible by 100 but not by 400), 2000 → True (divisible by 400).
questions.input_format:
Function signature: is_leap(year: int) -> bool
Parameters:
• year: a positive integer
Test format: each line of a test input is the argument list of one call (for example, 2024 means is_leap(2024)). The expected output is the repr of the returned value, one line per call.
questions.output_format: Return a bool: True or False.
hints: Check the divisibility by 400 first, then by 100, then by 4.
A one-line version: (year % 4 == 0 and year % 100 != 0) or year % 400 == 0.
Return the boolean value directly.
questions.reference_solution:
def is_leap(year):
    return (year % 4 == 0 and year % 100 != 0) or year % 400 == 0

extra_fields.input_format:
Function signature: is_leap(year: int) -> bool
Parameters:
• year: a positive integer
Test format: each line of a test input is the argument list of one call (for example, 2024 means is_leap(2024)). The expected output is the repr of the returned value, one line per call.
extra_fields.output_format: Return a bool: True or False.

questions.title: GCD and LCM Tuple Return
questions.objective: Return a tuple (gcd, lcm) for two integers using Euclidean algorithm.
questions.problem_statement:
Task: Write a function gcd_lcm(a, b) that returns both the GCD and the LCM of two positive integers as a tuple (gcd, lcm).
• GCD (greatest common divisor) is the largest number that divides both a and b
• Find the GCD with the Euclidean algorithm: while b is not 0, replace (a, b) by (b, a % b). When b becomes 0, the answer is a
• LCM (least common multiple) = original a x original b // gcd
• Do not use math.gcd
• Return the two values in this order: (gcd, lcm)

Example: gcd_lcm(12, 18) → (6, 36).
questions.input_format:
Function signature: gcd_lcm(a, b) -> tuple[int, int]
Parameters:
• a: a positive integer
• b: a positive integer
Test format: each line of a test input is the argument list of one call (for example, 12, 18 means gcd_lcm(12, 18)). The expected output is the repr of the returned value, one line per call.
questions.output_format: Return a tuple of two ints: (gcd, lcm).
hints: Keep copies of the original a and b, because the loop changes them.
Euclid loop: while b: a, b = b, a % b. The GCD is the final a.
lcm = original_a * original_b // gcd. Return (gcd, lcm).

extra_fields.input_format:
Function signature: gcd_lcm(a, b) -> tuple[int, int]
Parameters:
• a: a positive integer
• b: a positive integer
Test format: each line of a test input is the argument list of one call (for example, 12, 18 means gcd_lcm(12, 18)). The expected output is the repr of the returned value, one line per call.
extra_fields.output_format: Return a tuple of two ints: (gcd, lcm).

questions.title: Quadratic Equation Solver
questions.objective: Return real roots of ax^2 + bx + c = 0 as sorted tuple, or empty if complex.
questions.problem_statement:
Task: Write a function solve_quad(a, b, c) that returns the real roots of the equation ax^2 + bx + c = 0 as a tuple. The value of a is never 0.
• Discriminant: D = b^2 - 4ac
• If D < 0, there are no real roots: return an empty tuple ()
• If D == 0, there is one root: return a tuple with one value, (root,)
• If D > 0, there are two roots: return (smaller, larger)
• Roots are x = (-b +/- sqrt(D)) / (2a)
• Round every root to 4 decimal places

Examples: solve_quad(1, -3, 2) → (1.0, 2.0), solve_quad(1, 2, 1) → (-1.0,), solve_quad(1, 0, 1) → ().
questions.input_format:
Function signature: solve_quad(a, b, c) -> tuple
Parameters:
• a: coefficient of x^2 (non-zero integer)
• b: coefficient of x (integer)
• c: constant term (integer)
Test format: each line of a test input is the argument list of one call (for example, 1, -3, 2 means solve_quad(1, -3, 2)). The expected output is the repr of the returned value, one line per call.
questions.output_format: Return a tuple of floats: () or (root,) or (smaller, larger).
hints: Compute D = b * b - 4 * a * c first and decide the case from D.
Use math.sqrt(D). When a is negative the first root can be larger, so sort the two roots.
round(x, 4) + 0.0 turns a possible -0.0 into 0.0.

extra_fields.input_format:
Function signature: solve_quad(a, b, c) -> tuple
Parameters:
• a: coefficient of x^2 (non-zero integer)
• b: coefficient of x (integer)
• c: constant term (integer)
Test format: each line of a test input is the argument list of one call (for example, 1, -3, 2 means solve_quad(1, -3, 2)). The expected output is the repr of the returned value, one line per call.
extra_fields.output_format: Return a tuple of floats: () or (root,) or (smaller, larger).

questions.title: Safe Integer Conversion
questions.objective: Parse string to int, returning default fallback integer when conversion fails.
questions.problem_statement:
Task: Write a function safe_int(val, default=0) that converts a string to an integer, but never crashes.
• Try to convert val with int(val)
• If the conversion works, return the integer
• If the conversion fails (int() raises ValueError), return default instead
• Spaces around the number are fine: ' 77 ' → 77
• Text such as 'abc', '12.5' or an empty string cannot be converted, so the default is returned

Examples: safe_int('42') → 42, safe_int('abc') → 0, safe_int('12.5', default=-1) → -1.

Function signature: safe_int(val, default=0) -> int
Parameters:
• val: a string
• default: the integer to return when conversion fails (default 0)
Test format: each line of a test input is the argument list of one call (for example, '42' means safe_int('42')). The expected output is the repr of the returned value, one line per call.
questions.output_format: Return an int: the converted number or the default value.
hints: Put int(val) inside a try block.
Catch ValueError in the except block and return default there.
int() already accepts leading and trailing spaces and a + or - sign.

Function signature: safe_int(val, default=0) -> int
Parameters:
• val: a string
• default: the integer to return when conversion fails (default 0)
Test format: each line of a test input is the argument list of one call (for example, '42' means safe_int('42')). The expected output is the repr of the returned value, one line per call.
extra_fields.output_format: Return an int: the converted number or the default value.

questions.title: Temperature Scale Converter
questions.objective: Convert temperature between C, F, and K based on source and target unit codes.
questions.problem_statement:
Task: Write a function convert_temp(v, fr, to) that converts the temperature v from the unit fr to the unit to. The unit codes are 'C' (Celsius), 'F' (Fahrenheit) and 'K' (Kelvin).
• C to F: C x 9 / 5 + 32
• F to C: (F - 32) x 5 / 9
• C to K: C + 273.15
• K to C: K - 273.15
• For other pairs, convert to Celsius first, then to the target unit
• If fr and to are the same, the value stays the same
• If either unit code is not 'C', 'F' or 'K', raise ValueError
• Return the result rounded to 2 decimal places

Example: convert_temp(100, 'C', 'F') → 212.0.
questions.input_format:
Function signature: convert_temp(v, fr, to) -> float
Parameters:
• v: temperature value (number)
• fr: source unit code ('C', 'F' or 'K')
• to: target unit code ('C', 'F' or 'K')
Test format: each line of a test input is the argument list of one call (for example, 100, 'C', 'F' means convert_temp(100, 'C', 'F')). The expected output is the repr of the returned value, one line per call.
questions.output_format: Return a float rounded to 2 decimal places. For an invalid unit code, the call raises ValueError (the expected output line is ValueError).
questions.constraints:
-1000 <= v <= 10^6
Unit codes are single uppercase letters
hints: Use Celsius as the middle step: first convert v to Celsius, then convert Celsius to the target.
Validate both unit codes before converting, and raise ValueError(...) for a bad code.

questions.title: Permutations Formula
questions.objective: Compute permutations of N items taken R at a time using factorial functions.
questions.problem_statement:
Task: A permutation is an ordered arrangement. The number of ways to arrange r items chosen from n different items is written nPr.

Write a function perm_count(n, r) that returns nPr. Follow these rules:
• Formula: nPr = n! / (n - r)!
• n! (factorial) means 1 × 2 × 3 x ... x n, and 0! = 1
• Write your own helper function fact(k) that returns k!. You may use a loop or recursion. Do not use math.factorial
• Use fact() inside perm_count(), and use integer division (//) so the result stays an int
• If r is greater than n, there are no arrangements: return 0
• If n or r is negative, raise ValueError
• r = 0 gives 1, because there is exactly one way to choose nothing

Examples: perm_count(5, 2) → 20 (5 × 4), perm_count(5, 5) → 120, perm_count(5, 0) → 1, perm_count(3, 5) → 0.

questions.output_format: Return an int: the number of permutations. For a negative n or r, the call raises ValueError (the expected output line is ValueError).

fact(k) can be a loop: result = 1, then multiply by every number from 2 to k.

questions.title: Bisection Root Finder
questions.objective: Approximate square root of float N to 6 decimals using binary bisection.
questions.problem_statement:
Task: Bisection finds a square root by repeatedly cutting a search interval in half. Write a function sqrt_bisect(n, eps=1e-6) that approximates the square root of n without using math.sqrt() or **0.5. Follow these steps exactly, so that everyone gets the same answer.

Step 1: If n < 0, raise ValueError.
Step 2: Set low = 0.0 and high = max(1.0, n). (When n is between 0 and 1, its square root is larger than n, so high must be at least 1.)
Step 3: While high - low > eps, repeat:
• mid = (low + high) / 2
• If mid * mid < n, the root is in the upper half, so set low = mid
• Otherwise the root is in the lower half, so set high = mid
Step 4: Return round((low + high) / 2, 6).

Examples:
• sqrt_bisect(25) → 5.0
• sqrt_bisect(2) → 1.414214
• sqrt_bisect(0.25) → 0.5
• sqrt_bisect(2, eps=0.001) → 1.414551 (a larger eps stops earlier and gives a rougher answer)
questions.input_format:

Parameters:
• n: the number whose square root is needed (non-negative number)
• eps: required accuracy, the loop stops when the interval is not wider than eps (default 1e-6)
Test format: each line of a test input is the argument list of one call (for example, 25 means sqrt_bisect(25)). The expected output is the repr of the returned value, one line per call.
questions.output_format: Return a float: the approximate square root rounded to 6 decimal places. For a negative n, the call raises ValueError (the expected output line is ValueError).
hints: Each loop step halves the interval, so the loop needs only about log2((high - low) / eps) steps.
